protocols.title: Gram stain (ASM protocol, Gephardt et al. 1981 / ASMCUE 2005)

steps.action: Flood air-dried, heat-fixed smear of cells for 1 minute with crystal violet staining reagent.

parameters.name: reagent
parameters.value: crystal violet staining reagent (2 g crystal violet in 20 ml 95% ethanol + 0.8 g ammonium oxalate in 80 ml distilled water)

steps.caution: Please note that the quality of the smear (too heavy or too light cell concentration) will affect the Gram Stain results.

steps.action: Wash slide in a gentle and indirect stream of tap water for 2 seconds.
Flood slide with the mordant: Gram's iodine. Wait 1 minute.

parameters.name: reagent
parameters.value: Gram's iodine (1.0 g iodine, 2.0 g potassium iodide, 300 ml distilled water)

steps.action: Wash slide in a gentle and indirect stream of tap water for 2 seconds.
Flood slide with decolorizing agent. Wait 15 seconds or add drop by drop to slide until decolorizing agent running from the slide runs clear.

parameters.name: decolorizer
parameters.value: Ethanol, 95% (vol/vol); alternate: acetone 50 ml + ethanol (95%) 50 ml

steps.caution: The step that is most crucial in effecting the outcome of the stain is the decolorizing step. Over-decolorizing ... gram-positive cells may stain pink to red ... under-decolorizing ... gram-negative cells may appear blue to purple.

steps.action: Flood slide with counterstain, safranin. Wait 30 seconds to 1 minute.

parameters.name: reagent
parameters.value: safranin working solution (10 ml stock [2.5 g safranin O in 100 ml 95% ethanol] + 90 ml distilled water)

steps.action: Wash slide in a gentle and indirect stream of tap water until no color appears in the effluent and then blot dry with absorbent paper.
Observe the results of the staining procedure under oil immersion using a Brightfield microscope. Gram-negative bacteria will stain pink/red and gram-positive bacteria will stain blue/purple.
steps.caution: It is recommended that young, actively growing cultures be used for gram staining.

protocols.title: Gram stain (Hardy Diagnostics kit IFU)
protocols.appliesTo: Hardy Diagnostics Gram stain kits/reagents (methanol-fixed smears; decolorizers 25/50/75% acetone)

steps.action: Fix smear: methanol fix slide by flooding with absolute methanol (95%) for 1-2 minutes, then tilt the slide to drain off methanol and allow to air dry.
steps.caution: Note: Do not use heat fixation.

steps.action: Cover slide with Crystal Violet Reagent for one minute.
Rinse slide with deionized or tap water.
Cover slide with Iodine Reagent for one minute.
Gently rinse the slide with deionized or tap water and allow to drain.
Tilt the slide and flood with a few drops of Decolorizer until no violet color runs off. This will usually take 10 seconds or less depending on the thickness of the specimen.
steps.caution: Do not over decolorize.

steps.action: Rinse slide gently with deionized or tap water.
Cover slide with Safranin, Advanced Counterstain™, or Basic Fuchsin counterstain for one minute.
Rinse slide gently with deionized or tap water. The rinse water in this step should be slightly pink. Do not wash excessively. Allow slide to drain and air dry, or blot.
Examine slide under lens (1,000X magnification) using immersion oil.
"Heat-fix" the slide with the specimen by passing it over a heat source, such as a flame, several times. The slide should be passed very quickly through the flame and not be heated excessively.
Flood the fixed smear with crystal violet solution (#1) and allow to remain for 1 minute. Rinse with distilled or tap water.
Flood the slide with iodine solution (#2). Allow to remain for one minute. Rinse.
Holding slide on a tilt with a clothes pin, flood the slide with decolorizer (#3) for one to five seconds. Rinse.
Flood the slide with safranin (#4). Allow to remain for 30 seconds. Rinse.
Dry the slide on bibulous paper and examine under a 100X objective.

protocols.title: Autoclaving biohazardous liquids and waste (Virginia Tech EHS)
protocols.appliesTo: general (biohazardous liquids and dry waste in laboratory autoclaves)

steps.action: Collect liquid in glassware or plasticware that is suitable for autoclaving. Never autoclave plastic materials of uncertain heat stability.
steps.caution: Never autoclave plastic materials of uncertain heat stability.

steps.action: Do not fill containers more than 2/3 full.
Make sure that caps are loose or use vented closures.
steps.caution: Never put sealed containers in an autoclave. They can explode.

steps.action: Never put materials containing solvents, corrosives or radioactive materials in the autoclave (e.g., phenol, chloroform, pyridine, or bleach).
steps.caution: Prohibited: solvents, corrosives, radioactive materials, phenol, chloroform, pyridine, bleach.

steps.action: Set cycle: for both DRY and LIQUID biohazardous waste materials, cycle times must be set for a minimum of 30 minutes @ 121°C, 15 psi. Larger volumes of liquids and larger loads of solids require longer sterilization times (75 ml 25 min; 250 ml 30 min; 500 ml 40 min; 1000 ml 45 min; 1500 ml 50 min; 2000 ml 55 min; >2000 ml 55 + 10 min/L).
steps.caution: LIQUIDS MUST BE AUTOCLAVED WITH SLOW EXHAUST.

steps.action: After the cycle, slowly crack the door open no more than ½" and allow all steam to escape by waiting at least 10 minutes before unloading the material.
steps.caution: Material will still be HOT!

steps.action: Let liquids stand 10–20 minutes after the autoclave is opened.
steps.caution: Superheated liquids can boil over and damage the autoclave and cause personal injury.

protocols.title: Biohazardous spill inside a biological safety cabinet (UW EH&S)

steps.action: Do not turn off the BSC during spill clean-up. Do not place your head inside the cabinet or under the sash at any time.
Remove any contaminated sharp items from the spill using tongs or forceps. Do not use your hands. Place contaminated items in appropriate sharps container.
steps.caution: Do not use your hands.

steps.action: Cover spill with paper towels or absorbent material.

Slowly pour an appropriate decontaminant solution around the spill and allow to flow into the spill. A freshly prepared 1:10 dilution of household bleach (~0.5% sodium hypochlorite) is suitable for most biological spills.
steps.caution: Freshly prepared.

steps.action: Allow 30 minutes of contact time. The contact time may vary depending on the decontaminant used. Follow manufacturer's directions.
Wipe up spill, work surfaces, walls, and any equipment in the BSC with paper towels dampened with decontaminant. If using bleach, follow with a water rinse to protect metal surfaces from corrosion.
steps.caution: Bleach corrodes metal surfaces.

steps.action: Place contaminated paper towels and other clean-up materials in a biohazard bag.
steps.caution: Bleach may be incompatible with some radioactive materials, especially if they contain radioiodine.

protocols.title: High Efficiency Transformation Protocol (NEB 5-alpha, #C2987H/#C2987I)
protocols.appliesTo: NEB 5-alpha Competent E. coli (High Efficiency), NEB #C2987H (50 µl single-use vials) / #C2987I (200 µl format); the heat-shock timing is specific to NEB's transformation tube

steps.action: For C2987H, thaw a tube of NEB 5-alpha Competent E. coli cells on ice for 10 minutes. (For C2987I, thaw on ice until the last ice crystals disappear, mix gently and pipette 50 µl of cells into a transformation tube on ice.)
steps.caution: Store competent cells at -80°C. Storage at -20°C will result in a significant decrease in transformation efficiency.

steps.action: Add 1-5 µl containing 1 pg-100 ng of plasmid DNA to the cell mixture. Carefully flick the tube 4-5 times to mix cells and DNA. Do not vortex.
steps.caution: Do not vortex.

steps.action: Place the mixture on ice for 30 minutes. Do not mix.
steps.caution: Expect a 2-fold loss in transformation efficiency for every 10 minutes this step is shortened.

steps.action: Heat shock at exactly 42°C for exactly 30 seconds. Do not mix.
steps.caution: Both the temperature and the timing of the heat shock step are important and specific to the transformation volume and vessel. Using the transformation tube provided, 30 seconds at 42°C is optimal.

steps.action: Place on ice for 5 minutes. Do not mix.
Pipette 950 µl of room temperature SOC outgrowth media into the mixture.
Place at 37°C for 60 minutes. Shake vigorously (250 rpm) or rotate.
steps.caution: Expect a 2-fold loss in transformation efficiency for every 15 minutes this step is shortened.

steps.action: Warm selection plates to 37°C.
Mix the cells thoroughly by flicking the tube and inverting, then perform several 10-fold serial dilutions in SOC.
Spread 50-100 µl of each dilution onto a selection plate and incubate overnight at 37°C. Alternatively, incubate at 30°C for 24-36 hours or 25°C for 48 hours.

protocols.title: Bacterial Transformation (Addgene)
protocols.appliesTo: general chemically competent E. coli; Addgene notes 'For the highest transformation efficiency, we recommend that you follow the instructions that came with your competent cells.'

steps.action: Take competent cells out of -80°C and thaw on ice (approximately 20-30 mins).
Remove agar plates (containing the appropriate antibiotic) from storage at 4°C and let warm up to room temperature and then (optional) incubate in 37°C incubator.
Mix 1 - 5 μl of DNA (usually 10 pg - 100 ng) into 20-50 μL of competent cells in a microcentrifuge or falcon tube. GENTLY mix by flicking the bottom of the tube with your finger a few times.
Incubate the competent cell/DNA mixture on ice for 20-30 mins.

Heat shock each transformation tube by placing the bottom 1/2 to 2/3 of the tube into a 42°C water bath for 30-60 secs (45 secs is usually ideal, but this varies depending on the competent cells you are using).
steps.caution: Varies depending on the competent cells you are using.

steps.action: Put the tubes back on ice for 2 min.
Add 250-1,000 μl LB or SOC media (without antibiotic) to the bacteria and grow in 37°C shaking incubator for 45 min.
steps.caution: This step is not critical for Ampicillin resistance but is much more important for other antibiotic resistances.

steps.action: Plate some or all of the transformation onto a 10 cm LB agar plate containing the appropriate antibiotic.
Incubate plates at 37°C overnight.

recipes.name: LB broth (Miller)
recipes.steps: Sigma L3522 (premixed powder): 1. Suspend 25 g in 1 L of distilled water. 2. Autoclave for 15 minutes at 121 °C. Allow to cool before making additions, such as antibiotics (if desired). From scratch (CSH Protocols, same composition, labelled only 'LB'): combine reagents in 950 mL H2O, shake to dissolve, adjust pH to 7.0 with 5 N NaOH (~0.2 mL), adjust volume to 1 L with H2O.
recipes.sterilization: Sigma: autoclave for 15 minutes at 121 °C. CSH: autoclaving for 20 min at 15 psi (1.05 kg/cm2) on liquid cycle.
recipes.notes: Sigma pH spec: 6.8-7.2 (2.5% solution). CSH Protocols' 'LB (Luria-Bertani) liquid medium' does not say Miller, but its 10 g/L NaCl matches Miller. Sigma variant for LC broth: 'Aseptically add 25 ml of sterile 0.1 M calcium chloride after autoclaving.'

recipes.name: LB broth (Lennox)
recipes.steps: 1. Suspend 20 g in 1 L of distilled water. 2. Autoclave for 15 minutes at 121 °C. To prepare Lennox L Broth: Add 1 g glucose and proceed with preparation instructions as above.
recipes.notes: Sigma: 'This nutrient-rich microbial broth contains peptides, amino acids and carbohydrates in a low-salt formulation.' Variant (Enquist and Sternberg): 'Aseptically add 10 ml of sterile 1 M magnesium sulfate after autoclaving.'

recipes.name: LB broth (Luria, low salt)
aliases: Luria Broth (Miller's Modification) [Sigma-listed synonym; conflicts with Miller = 10 g/L NaCl]
recipes.steps: 1. Suspend 15.5 g in 1 L of distilled water. 2. Autoclave for 15 minutes at 121°C. Allow to cool before making additions, such as antibiotics (if desired).
recipes.notes: Sigma pH spec 6.8-7.2 (1.55% solution); 'very low-salt formulation'. CAUTION: Sigma's own synonym list for this 0.5 g/L NaCl product includes 'Luria Broth (Miller's Modification)', while Sigma's Miller product (L3522) is 10 g/L NaCl — never resolve a recipe by name alone; check NaCl g/L.

recipes.name: LB agar (Miller)
recipes.steps: 1. Suspend 40 g in 1L of distilled water. 2. Heat to boiling while stirring to dissolve. 3. Autoclave for 15 minutes at 121°C. 4. Cool to 50°C prior to dispensing into sterile petri dishes.
recipes.notes: Addgene's LB agar premix uses 12.0 g agar-agar per litre (37 g premix: 10 g peptone from casein, 5 g yeast extract, 10 g NaCl, 12 g agar) and autoclaves at least 121 ℃ under 20 psi for at least 30 min; Addgene cools molten agar to 60 ℃ before adding antibiotic.

recipes.name: LB agar (Addgene premix; salt level = Miller, not named)
recipes.steps: Measure 37g of pre-mixed LB-agar powder per L of molten agar you'd like to make. Transfer powder into a bottle (400 mL agar in 1 L bottles; 200 mL in 500 mL bottles), add sterile water, swirl. Cover loosely (no air-tight seal), autoclave tape. Autoclave; cool in 60 ℃ water bath at least 5 min; add antibiotic (1000x stock); swirl; pour.
recipes.sterilization: Place the gel mix in the autoclave and run on a setting that gets the sample to at least 121 ℃ under 20 psi for at least 30 min.
recipes.notes: Addgene calls it 'Luria broth (LB)' without saying Miller/Lennox; NaCl 10 g/L corresponds to Miller. Agar 12 g/L differs from Sigma L3147's 15 g/L.

recipes.name: Phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), 1X
recipes.steps: Dissolve the reagents listed above in 800 mL of H2O. Adjust the pH to 7.4 (or 7.2, if required) with HCl, and then add H2O to 1 L. Dispense the solution into aliquots.
recipes.sterilization: Sterilize them by autoclaving for 20 min at 15 psi (1.05 kg/cm2) on liquid cycle or by filter sterilization. Store PBS at room temperature.
recipes.notes: Final 1×: 137 mM NaCl, 2.7 mM KCl, 10 mM Na2HPO4, 1.8 mM KH2PO4. 10× stock: 80 g NaCl, 2 g KCl, 14.4 g Na2HPO4, 2.4 g KH2PO4 per L. Optional supplements (1×): CaCl2•2H2O 0.133 g (1 mM), MgCl2•6H2O 0.10 g (0.5 mM). The page does not state the hydration form of Na2HPO4; 1.44 g = 10 mM corresponds to the anhydrous salt (inferred from the stated molarity, not stated by the source) — a hydrate would need a different mass.

reagents.name: Ethidium bromide (powder, Sigma E7637)
reagents.storage: Storage Class | 6.1A - Combustible acute toxic Cat. 1 and 2 / very toxic hazardous materials

claims.statement: Flood air-dried, heat-fixed smear of cells for 1 minute with crystal violet staining reagent.
claims.ruling: ASM, Hardy and Cornell all agree on 1 minute.

claims.statement: Flood slide with the mordant: Gram's iodine. Wait 1 minute.
claims.ruling: ASM, Hardy and Cornell all agree on 1 minute.

claims.statement: Flood slide with decolorizing agent. Wait 15 seconds or add drop by drop to slide until decolorizing agent running from the slide runs clear
claims.ruling: Hardy says ≤10 s with acetone-containing decolorizer and Cornell says 1-5 s; time depends on decolorizer strength and smear thickness — end-point 'runs clear' is the common criterion.

claims.statement: Some individuals will flood the slide for 15 seconds or less with decolorzing agent, while others recommend adding decolorizing agent drop wise for 5- 15 seconds or until the color of the decolorizing agent running from the slide no longer shows any color.
claims.ruling: ASM itself presents a range; consistent with Hardy (≤10 s) at the short end.

claims.statement: Tilt the slide and flood with a few drops of Decolorizer until no violet color runs off. This will usually take 10 seconds or less depending on the thickness of the specimen. Do not over decolorize.
claims.ruling: Faster acetone decolorizers need shorter times than ASM's 95% ethanol 15 s.

claims.statement: Holding slide on a tilt with a clothes pin, flood the slide with decolorizer (#3) for one to five seconds.
claims.appliesWhen: Cornell AHDC diagnostic smears (decolorizer composition not stated on page)
claims.ruling: Shortest of the three sources; ASM's 15 s with this decolorizer could over-decolorize.

claims.statement: Flood slide with counterstain, safranin. Wait 30 seconds to 1 minute.
claims.ruling: Hardy says one minute and Cornell 30 seconds; both inside ASM's range.

claims.statement: Methanol fix slide by flooding with absolute methanol (95%) for 1-2 minutes ... Note: Do not use heat fixation.
claims.ruling: ASM and Cornell use heat-fixed smears; Hardy argues methanol gives 'greater control over the decolorization process'. Both are in use; follow the kit IFU.

claims.statement: Never put materials containing solvents, corrosives or radioactive materials in the autoclave (e.g., phenol, chloroform, pyridine, or bleach).
claims.value: solvents, corrosives, radioactive materials, phenol, chloroform, pyridine, bleach
claims.ruling: Agrees with UNC ('Do not autoclave liquid wastes that contain bleach or ethanol'; 'Never autoclave live animals or any toxic, volatile, corrosive, or radioactive materials') and Stanford ('Do not autoclave items containing corrosives, solvents, volatiles or radioactive materials').

claims.statement: Never autoclave live animals or any toxic, volatile, corrosive, or radioactive materials. Do not autoclave liquid wastes that contain bleach or ethanol.
claims.value: live animals, toxic, volatile, corrosive, radioactive materials; liquid waste with bleach or ethanol
claims.ruling: Consistent with VT and Stanford lists.

claims.statement: Never put sealed containers in an autoclave. They can explode. Large bottles with narrow necks may also explode or boil over if filled too full of liquid.
claims.ruling: Stanford likewise: 'Never seal a container of liquid with a cork that may cause a pressurized explosion inside the autoclave.'

claims.statement: Set the cycle for 30 minutes, 121 degrees F at 20 PSI (or alternate required conditions depending on waste)
claims.ruling: Source text says '121 degrees F', which is not a sterilizing temperature; every other source (and Stanford's own context) uses 121 °C — treat as a typo, and note 20 psi vs the 15 psi used by VT/MIT/UCSD/CSH.

claims.statement: Liquid media requires a shorter cycle, often 15- 20 minutes while autoclavable medical waste requires a minimum of 30 minutes in order to be effectively sterilized
claims.appliesWhen: (small volumes of) liquid media vs bagged waste

claims.statement: A freshly prepared 1:10 dilution of household bleach (~0.5% sodium hypochlorite) is suitable for most biological spills.
claims.ruling: Agrees with CDC (1:10 final for large blood spills), UCSB, WVU, Case, USU, and WHO's 5000 ppm 'dirty conditions' level.

claims.statement: Typically, a solution of sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl) containing 1000 ppm (parts per million) available chlorine will be suitable for general surface disinfection, but stronger solutions (for example, 5000 ppm or 10 000 ppm) are recommended when dealing with heavy contamination
claims.ruling: WHO Table 2.2: 5% available-chlorine NaOCl solution 20 mL (clean, 1000 ppm) vs 100 mL (dirty, 5000 ppm); 1:10 household bleach ≈ 5000 ppm per CDC.

claims.statement: a 1:10 dilution of household bleach provides about 5250–6150 ppm.
claims.ruling: Bridges CDC/university '1:10' with WHO's ppm-based guidance.

claims.parameter: bleach dilution for small blood spills

notes: All values were copied from live pages/PDFs retrieved 2026-10-04 (UTC); nothing was filled in from memory. Unreachable / limitations: (1) CSH Protocols' 'Media containing agar or agarose' recipe and the CSH CaCl2 transformation protocol (pdb.prot3932, the usual 90 s heat-shock source) are behind a sign-in wall, so no 90 s heat-shock claim from a reputable source is recorded — only NEB 30 s, Thermo 30 s and Addgene 45 s (30-60 s). (2) WHO LBM4 core manual and its Decontamination monograph give ppm-based hypochlorite strengths (1000 ppm clean / 5000-10000 ppm dirty) but NO fixed bleach contact time; CDC's chemical-disinfectants page likewise gives dilutions (1:10 / 1:100) but no contact time for spills — contact times come only from university SOPs (15-20, 20, 30 min; USU also says 5 min). (3) WHO Table 2.2 lists '20 mL' / '100 mL' of 5% NaOCl for clean/dirty conditions without printing the per-litre unit for that row (other rows are g/L). (4) Sigma product pages and the Thermo SYBR Safe page redirected to regional (/NG/, /ng/) versions; the US URLs are recorded. (5) The Fisher BP1302 SDS prints hazard statements as text without H-codes ('Toxic if inhaled' = Acute Inhal. Tox. Cat. 3); no H-codes were inferred. Thermo's SYBR Safe page gives no GHS classification, CAS or storage condition, so those fields are null. (6) CSH PBS does not state the hydration form of Na2HPO4; 1.44 g for 10 mM implies anhydrous (inference, flagged in recipe notes). (7) Stanford's biosafety manual literally says '121 degrees F' for its waste cycle — an evident typo for °C, recorded as disputed. (8) 'LB' ambiguity: CSH and Addgene both say just 'LB'/'Luria broth' with 10 g/L NaCl (Miller composition); Sigma lists 'Luria Broth (Miller's Modification)' as a synonym of its 0.5 g/L NaCl low-salt product L3397. Always resolve LB variant by NaCl g/L. (9) A University of Wisconsin-La Crosse autoclave table surfaced in search (different minutes per volume) but its PDF returned 404, so it was not used.
